title: Housing policy & residential choice
summary: Evaluating how ZIP code-level rent standards relate to housing voucher concentration and access to neighborhoods.
question: How did the 2018 Small Area Fair Market Rent policy change the residential concentration of Housing Choice Voucher households?
approach: Constructed a 2014–2022 census-tract panel from HUD housing data and compared Dallas County with Harris County.
Used difference-in-differences with tract and year fixed effects, alongside event-study checks and geospatial analysis.
Examined changes in voucher concentration and patterns across neighborhood racial composition and poverty.
takeaway: The analysis finds an association between the policy change and lower voucher concentration in the treatment area. Interpreting that pattern requires looking beyond a single estimate to pre-policy trends and the limits of the available data.
limitation: Pre-policy trend differences complicate causal interpretation. HUD suppresses small household counts, and the data do not track where individual households relocate.
credits: Team: Lingyue Hao, He Jiang, Ammy Lin, Myla Simmons, and Anvita Suresh.

title: Learning with fewer connections
summary: Comparing static sparsity, SET, and RigL to study the relationship between neural network capacity and predictive performance.
question: How much can a neural network’s connectivity be reduced while retaining useful predictive performance?
approach: Compared fixed sparse masks, Sparse Evolutionary Training, and gradient-guided RigL on a CIFAR-style ResNet-20.
Evaluated 90%, 95%, and 98% sparsity under SGD with momentum and Adam.
Inspected accuracy curves, weight visualizations, and connectivity changes across the training runs.
takeaway: Static sparsity remained a competitive baseline, while RigL generally outperformed SET. Optimizer choice affected the comparison, and the highest sparsity level exposed clear capacity limits.
limitation: These experiments used 15 training epochs, one model family, and CIFAR-10 without data augmentation. The comparisons describe this experimental setting rather than a universal ranking of sparsity methods.
credits: Team: Ammy Lin, Tonantzin Real Rojas, and Anvita Suresh. Completed for Introduction to Deep Learning at Duke University.

title: From listening data to recommendations
summary: An end-to-end music recommendation prototype connecting data ingestion, scheduled model workflows, and an interactive dashboard.
role: Exploratory analysis, Airflow DAGs, Streamlit dashboard, recommendation model, and team coordination, shared with teammates as documented in the repository.
question: What does it take to turn track metadata and a small amount of listening history into a repeatable recommendation workflow?
approach: Combined public track metadata with generated users and synthetic listening events.
Used Airflow to orchestrate data ingestion, embedding generation, and recommendation updates in a PostgreSQL-backed pipeline.
Presented results through a Streamlit dashboard, with Python tests and workflow-level validation supporting the pipeline.
takeaway: The prototype connects the modeling step with the engineering around it: data preparation, scheduled inference, persistence, validation, and a usable interface for exploring recommendations.
limitation: Listening histories are simulated. The content-based model does not establish recommendation quality for real users, and the synchronous inference approach has not been validated for large user populations.
credits: Team: Jordan, Aesha, Ammy, and Tonantzin. The repository documents shared responsibilities for the model, orchestration, dashboard, and testing.

image_caption: The recommendation dashboard from the project repository, using the prototype’s generated listening activity.

title: Interpretable flood-risk modeling
summary: A synthetic-data proof of concept exploring predictive accuracy, robustness, and interpretable triggers for parametric flood insurance.
role: Project Manager and Risk Strategist, as documented in the project’s contributor roles.
question: How can a flood-risk model balance predictive performance with interpretable and robust payout-trigger rules?
approach: Benchmarked linear regression, XGBoost, and sparse optimal decision trees across 20 environmental, infrastructure, land-use, and governance features.
Explored feature importance with SHAP and evaluated sensitivity to reporting bias and shifted feature distributions.
Simulated tiered payout rules and compared trigger thresholds for different stakeholder priorities.
takeaway: The proof of concept makes the tradeoffs between accuracy, interpretability, data quality, and stakeholder priorities explicit. It connects model evaluation to the decisions that a predictive system might support.
limitation: This project uses synthetic data. Its feature rankings and payout rules are experimental and require validation on credible real-world data before supporting insurance or disaster-response decisions.
credits: Team: Lingyue Hao, He Jiang, Ammy Lin, Myla Simmons, and Anvita Suresh. Completed for IDS 705: Machine Learning at Duke University.

title: Understanding portfolio tail risk
summary: Using a Vasicek one-factor model and Monte Carlo simulation to study how correlated defaults shape credit portfolio losses.
question: How do default probabilities and dependence between borrowers change the distribution of credit portfolio losses?
approach: Used the public Default of Credit Card Clients dataset as the portfolio basis.
Modeled defaults through a shared systematic factor and borrower-specific factors in the Vasicek framework.
Simulated loss distributions under alternative default-probability and correlation assumptions, comparing Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk.
takeaway: The simulations show why expected loss alone does not describe portfolio stress: changing default dependence can alter the tail of the loss distribution substantially.
limitation: Results depend on the one-factor model, selected scenario assumptions, and a historical dataset. They are a classroom simulation, not a forecast of current credit losses.
credits: Team: Jordan Andrew, Ammy Lin, Farnoosh Memari, and Tonantzin Real Rojas. Completed for MATH 789 at Duke University.

title: The DNA dilemma
summary: A classroom ethics simulation exploring genetic data privacy, consent, and competing responsibilities through four stakeholder perspectives.
role: Co-designed classroom scenarios and co-led the discussion with Tonantzin Real Rojas. The repository credits Gemini-assisted implementation of the web experience.
question: How do decisions about genetic data change when viewed from the perspective of a consumer, executive, buyer, or data scientist?
approach: Designed four stakeholder paths around a hypothetical genetic-data sale and its consequences.
Used branching choices to surface tensions between consent, privacy, research value, and organizational obligations.
Added reflection prompts and a personal decision recap to support classroom discussion.
takeaway: The simulation makes ethical tradeoffs tangible by asking participants to choose, revisit their assumptions, and compare how responsibility looks from another stakeholder’s perspective.
limitation: The scenarios are hypothetical teaching material inspired by real events. They are designed for ethical reflection, not as a factual reconstruction or legal analysis of the 23andMe case.
credits: Discussion and scenario design: Ammy Lin and Tonantzin Real Rojas. Developed for IDS 704: Data Science Ethics and Policy at Duke University, with AI-assisted web implementation.
